items.prompt: What does 'fidelity' mean when talking about a design prototype?
choices: How expensive the specific prototyping tool or software license happened to be for the team to purchase and use
How closely the prototype resembles the finished product, in look, behavior, or response speed
How many individual screens or distinct states the resulting prototype ends up containing once it's finished
How many separate people were actually recruited to sit down and test the prototype once it was built
items.explanation: Fidelity is about resemblance to the real thing — visually, behaviorally, or in responsiveness. It has nothing to do with tool cost or the number of testers; a one-screen coded interaction can be higher fidelity than a fifty-screen static mockup.
items.reference:
📝 Paper — minutes, tests structure
🖼️ Wireframe — hours, tests layout/wording
🖱️ Clickable — days, tests the flow end to end
💻 Coded — weeks, tests real interaction/performance

Why: fidelity is a spectrum — cost and realism rise together as you move up it.

items.prompt: A prototype looks pixel-perfect and realistic, but doesn't respond to a single tap. What can you say about its fidelity?
choices: It's high fidelity overall in this case, since fidelity as a concept is really mainly about visual appearance
It can be high visual fidelity while being low behavioral fidelity — the two aren't the same dial
It's automatically considered low fidelity here simply because it isn't built out of finished, shippable code
Fidelity as a concept genuinely only ever applies meaningfully to prototypes that are built using real code
items.explanation: Fidelity isn't a single dial. A prototype can be highly realistic in appearance while being completely fake in behavior, or the reverse — an ugly gray-box screen that behaves exactly like the real feature will.
items.reference:
📝 Paper — minutes, tests structure
🖼️ Wireframe — hours, tests layout/wording
🖱️ Clickable — days, tests the flow end to end
💻 Coded — weeks, tests real interaction/performance

Why: fidelity is a spectrum — cost and realism rise together as you move up it.

items.prompt: Which pair correctly separates the two things 'fidelity' can independently describe?
choices: Speed of construction and raw dollar cost to build — two different axes of how expensive a prototype was to make
Look/feel (visual realism) and behavior/response (does it actually act like the real thing)
Number of screens included and number of testers recruited — two different axes of how big the study itself was
Tool used to build it and total time spent building it — two different axes of how the team worked, not what it shows
items.explanation: Visual realism and behavioral realism are separate axes. A prototype can be strong on one and weak on the other — knowing which axis a question needs is exactly what later levels build on.
items.reference:
📝 Paper — minutes, tests structure
🖼️ Wireframe — hours, tests layout/wording
🖱️ Clickable — days, tests the flow end to end
💻 Coded — weeks, tests real interaction/performance

Why: fidelity is a spectrum — cost and realism rise together as you move up it.

items.prompt: A team wants to know if the *order* of steps in a signup flow makes sense to a first-time user. What's the minimum fidelity that can answer that?
choices: A coded, fully live-wired version connected to real backend data and real production-grade performance characteristics
A paper sketch or clickable prototype — the question is about structure, not real motion or data
Nothing short of actually shipping the real feature to real users in production can honestly answer this question
A polished, pixel-perfect static mockup with every visual detail finished but no actual click-through behavior at all
items.explanation: Order-of-steps is a structural question. It doesn't depend on real motion, real data, or real performance, so a paper sketch or a clickable prototype is enough to answer it — reaching further costs more without buying a better answer.
items.reference:
A prototype's job is to answer one question, as cheaply as the question allows.

Why: picking more fidelity than a question needs wastes time; picking less can't answer it at all.

items.prompt: Why is 'always use the cheapest possible prototype' not the right rule to follow?
choices: It is in fact the right rule to follow here — cheaper is, in every situation, always strictly the better choice
Because some questions (like how a drag gesture feels) genuinely can't be answered without enough real behavior to feel
Because cheap, rough-looking prototypes always come across as unprofessional and unconvincing to watching stakeholders
Because only prototypes built with real, production-quality code are considered genuine prototypes in the first place
items.explanation: The goal isn't minimum cost for its own sake — it's matching fidelity to what the question actually needs. Some questions, especially about interaction feel or performance, require enough real behavior that a cheap prototype simply can't produce a trustworthy answer.
items.reference:
A prototype's job is to answer one question, as cheaply as the question allows.

Why: picking more fidelity than a question needs wastes time; picking less can't answer it at all.

items.prompt: A designer picks a fidelity level 'because that's what we always use,' without asking what the current question needs. What's the risk?
choices: There's genuinely no risk here at all — staying consistent with past habits is always a good, safe default to follow
The fidelity might not match the question, either wasting effort on unnecessary realism or missing something the test needed to catch
This mismatch only really matters in situations where the team happens to be testing with genuinely real users
This particular risk only ever applies specifically to prototypes that are built using real, production-quality code
items.explanation: Fidelity should follow from the specific question being asked, not from habit. A default choice can easily be too much (wasted cost) or too little (a question the test can't actually answer) for the situation at hand.
items.reference:
A prototype's job is to answer one question, as cheaply as the question allows.

Why: picking more fidelity than a question needs wastes time; picking less can't answer it at all.

items.prompt: Roughly how does build cost change as you move from a clickable prototype to a fully coded one?
choices: It stays roughly about the same the whole way, regardless of how far along the fidelity spectrum you happen to move
It rises sharply — a coded prototype typically costs far more than a clickable one, for a smaller jump in trustworthiness
It actually gets noticeably cheaper as you go, since code written for a prototype can usually be reused directly later
Build cost, as a factor, really has nothing meaningful to do with where a prototype sits on the fidelity spectrum
items.explanation: Cost rises much faster than fidelity climbs the spectrum, especially at the top end. Going from clickable to coded is usually the biggest cost jump of all, while the trustworthiness gain is comparatively smaller.
items.reference:
Low fidelity

Minutes to days, cheap to redo

High fidelity

Weeks, expensive to redo

Why: cost rises sharply as fidelity climbs — the cheap end is where most wrong ideas should get caught.

items.prompt: Why does it matter that a paper sketch is 'cheap to redo'?
choices: It genuinely doesn't matter much here — having to redo an early prototype from scratch is actually fairly rare in practice
Because when a cheap test reveals a wrong idea, fixing and retesting costs almost nothing, so wrong ideas get caught before they're expensive
Because paper, as a raw physical material, happens to be considerably more durable over time than any digital screen
Because prototypes sketched on paper specifically don't ever need to be shown to or tested with real people at all
items.explanation: The value of a cheap prototype isn't just its low upfront cost — it's that being wrong at that stage is nearly free to recover from. That's what makes catching mistakes early so much cheaper than catching them late.
items.reference:
Low fidelity

Minutes to days, cheap to redo

High fidelity

Weeks, expensive to redo

Why: cost rises sharply as fidelity climbs — the cheap end is where most wrong ideas should get caught.

items.prompt: What is a 'feedback loop' in the context of prototyping?
choices: A single, formal meeting where designers on a team sit down together and critique each other's existing work
The repeating cycle of showing a prototype to a real person, learning from their reaction, and deciding what to change next
Simply another, more casual way the unit refers interchangeably to the broader concept of a 'user interview'
The overall process of taking a validated design and translating it carefully into real, shippable production code
items.explanation: A feedback loop is the repeatable cycle: build just enough to test, show it to someone real, learn from what happens, and use that to decide the next step — often looping again with a refined version.
items.reference:
Show it→Watch/ask→Decide

Why: testing before building is what lets a wrong idea get caught while it's still cheap to fix.

items.prompt: Why does a cheaper prototype tend to allow *more* feedback loops within the same project timeline?
choices: It genuinely doesn't — how many loops a team can run has essentially nothing to do with how much each one costs
Because a fast, cheap build-test cycle can repeat several times in the time one expensive build would take
Because prototypes that are cheap to build apparently don't require being tested with any real users at all
Because prototypes that are expensive and time-consuming to build are, as a rule, simply never tested at all
items.explanation: Loop length tracks build cost. A prototype that takes days instead of weeks to build and test lets a team run the cycle multiple times — catching and fixing more wrong turns — within the same overall timeline.
items.reference:
Show it→Watch/ask→Decide

Why: testing before building is what lets a wrong idea get caught while it's still cheap to fix.

items.prompt: A team skips testing entirely and builds their idea straight into the live product. What have they given up?
choices: Nothing of real value — testing a rough idea before building it is, in the end, really just optional busywork
The chance to catch a wrong idea while it's still cheap to fix, before real engineering time is spent on it
Only the chance to impress watching stakeholders with an early, polished-looking demo of the finished feature
The underlying ability to ever meaningfully change or revise that particular feature again at any point later on
items.explanation: Skipping the loop doesn't just skip a formality — it removes the one chance to discover a flawed idea while fixing it is still nearly free, before the expensive build happens.
items.reference:
Show it→Watch/ask→Decide

Why: testing before building is what lets a wrong idea get caught while it's still cheap to fix.

items.prompt: Is a clickable Figma prototype meant to eventually become the shipped feature?
choices: Yes, prototypes like this one are generally always gradually upgraded piece by piece into the final shipped product
No — it's a throwaway stand-in built to get an answer; the real feature is usually built separately afterward
Only if the usability test it was built for happens to succeed — a failed test means it gets discarded entirely instead
Prototypes and the eventual shipped feature are, in every case, always built and maintained inside the exact same file
items.explanation: A prototype's purpose is to produce an answer as cheaply as possible, not to survive into production. Treating it as a smaller version of the final build usually means it wasn't cheap enough to build in the first place.
items.reference:
A prototype is a throwaway stand-in — not a smaller version of the final product.

Why: a prototype exists to get an answer, not to become the shipped feature.

items.prompt: A stakeholder says, 'why build a throwaway prototype at all — just build a smaller version of the real feature.' What's the flaw in that suggestion?
choices: There's genuinely no flaw in that reasoning at all — that is in fact exactly what a good prototype should actually be
A 'smaller version of the real feature' still carries real-feature costs (real code, real integration) that a true prototype is specifically built to avoid
Prototypes, properly built, are in fact never meaningfully smaller in scope than the real, fully shipped feature itself
This particular concern genuinely only ever matters when the prototype in question happens to be built using real code
items.explanation: The whole point of a prototype is to answer a question without paying real-feature costs. A 'smaller real feature' still touches real code and real integration — it's not actually cheap, which defeats the reason to prototype in the first place.
items.reference:
A prototype is a throwaway stand-in — not a smaller version of the final product.

Why: a prototype exists to get an answer, not to become the shipped feature.

items.prompt: In the feedback loop, what happens right after 'learn' if the reaction was 'wrong or unclear'?
choices: The team decides to ship the feature anyway, treating the unclear reaction as close enough to a passing result
The loop returns to the idea/open-question step, rather than advancing to higher fidelity or shipping
The entire project gets formally cancelled outright, since an unclear reaction is treated as a hard stop signal
Nothing at all happens next — an outcome of 'wrong or unclear' simply ends the loop permanently right there
items.explanation: A 'wrong or unclear' result sends the loop back to refine the idea, not forward. Only a confirmed answer justifies moving to the next step — raising fidelity or building for real.
items.reference:
Idea→Build enough to test→Show a real person→Learn→Decide next step

Why: the loop only advances to a higher fidelity or a real build once an answer is confirmed enough to justify it.

items.prompt: What decides whether the loop moves toward 'raise fidelity' or toward 'ship it for real' after a confirmed result?
choices: A fixed, pre-agreed number of loops that the team has decided in advance must always run before any decision is made
Whether the confidence gained is now enough to justify the cost of the next, more expensive step
Whichever specific option the engineering team on the project happens to personally prefer at that point in time
The loop, once a result is confirmed, always moves straight to 'ship it for real' regardless of what was actually learned
items.explanation: There's no fixed loop count — the decision is whether the confidence just gained is worth what the next, pricier step would cost. Sometimes that's another round at higher fidelity; sometimes it's enough to build for real.
items.reference:
Idea→Build enough to test→Show a real person→Learn→Decide next step

Why: the loop only advances to a higher fidelity or a real build once an answer is confirmed enough to justify it.

items.prompt: A team that jumps straight to a coded prototype without running any cheaper round first is best described as:
choices: Using the loop exactly as it was originally intended to be used, just happening to start at a slightly different point
Paying for the most expensive step in the loop first, before running any cheap steps that might have answered the same question
Skipping the entire feedback loop altogether — in this framing, no loop of any kind was genuinely ever used here
Genuinely impossible to evaluate fairly at all without first knowing how the eventual coded test actually turned out
items.explanation: They're still inside a loop, but they entered it at its most expensive point, which is what the L3 checkout story pays for — a cheap round could very likely have answered the same question for a fraction of the cost.
items.reference:
Idea→Build enough to test→Show a real person→Learn→Decide next step

Why: the loop only advances to a higher fidelity or a real build once an answer is confirmed enough to justify it.

items.prompt: A team wants to know if a new drag-to-reorder gesture feels responsive and natural. What type of question is this, and what fidelity does it need?
choices: Structural — a plain paper sketch with no real motion at all is already fully sufficient to answer this question
Interaction feel — it needs a prototype with real, running interaction, since motion can't be faked by static or click-through screens
Performance — this specific question requires testing against genuine, full-scale production data volume to answer
None of these three categories genuinely apply at all to a question about a drag gesture's feel or responsiveness
items.explanation: Feel-of-motion questions are interaction-feel questions. A click-through can fake the destination state but not the motion getting there, so answering this honestly requires a prototype with real, running interaction.
items.reference:
Question typeMinimum fidelity
StructuralPaper / clickable
Interaction feelReal running interaction
Performance / scaleReal or near-real build

Why: the type of question, not its perceived importance, determines the minimum fidelity that can answer it.

items.prompt: A team wants to know whether a list view stays usable when it has 50,000 real rows instead of the 20 sample rows in their mockup. What type of question is this?
choices: Structural — this is fundamentally a question about whether the steps and layout are arranged in a sensible order
Interaction feel — this is fundamentally a question about whether the motion and timing of an interaction feels right
Performance/scale — this needs real or near-real data and conditions, which no amount of visual fidelity can substitute for
This isn't actually a valid or meaningful prototyping question at all, given how the team happened to phrase it
items.explanation: Behavior under real data volume and real conditions is a performance/scale question. It can't be answered by visual polish or click-through fidelity — only something running against real or near-real conditions will show it.
items.reference:
Question typeMinimum fidelity
StructuralPaper / clickable
Interaction feelReal running interaction
Performance / scaleReal or near-real build

Why: the type of question, not its perceived importance, determines the minimum fidelity that can answer it.

items.prompt: Why is it a mistake to assume 'more important feature' automatically means 'needs higher fidelity to test'?
choices: It's genuinely not a mistake at all here — how important a feature feels always directly determines its needed fidelity
Because the minimum fidelity needed depends on the *type* of question (structural, interaction-feel, performance), not on how important the feature feels
Because features that are considered genuinely important, by definition, never actually need to be tested at all first
Because fidelity, as a concept, is really only ever about a prototype's visual polish, not about its real importance
items.explanation: Importance affects how much it costs to be wrong, but not what kind of test can catch that wrongness. An important feature with a purely structural question still only needs a cheap prototype — reaching higher buys no extra insight.
items.reference:
Question typeMinimum fidelity
StructuralPaper / clickable
Interaction feelReal running interaction
Performance / scaleReal or near-real build

Why: the type of question, not its perceived importance, determines the minimum fidelity that can answer it.

items.prompt: A project has six weeks before a launch decision. Why does a three-week build loop leave the team worse off than a two-day loop, even if both eventually surface the same problem?
choices: It genuinely doesn't leave them worse off at all — the eventual outcome ends up being exactly the same either way
The three-week loop leaves no time to act on what's learned, while the two-day loop leaves time to fix the problem and retest, still inside the six weeks
A three-week build is, by default, always considered meaningfully higher quality regardless of what it ends up revealing
Loop length, as a factor, genuinely has no real relationship at all to a project's fixed upcoming deadline or timeline
items.explanation: Loop length determines how many rounds fit inside a fixed deadline. A three-week loop in a six-week window allows exactly one round with no time to recover from a bad result; a two-day loop leaves room to fix and retest multiple times.
items.reference:
A fixed timeline holds more short loops than long ones — loop length trades directly against how many chances you get to catch a mistake.

Why: a shorter loop isn't just cheaper per round — it buys more rounds inside the same deadline.

items.prompt: What's the main reason a team would deliberately choose a slightly higher-fidelity prototype even though it shortens how many loops they can run?
choices: Higher fidelity is, in essentially every situation, always strictly better, so this never really counts as a real trade-off
Because the question being asked genuinely needs that fidelity to be answered at all — fewer, trustworthy loops beat many loops that can't answer the real question
Mainly just to make the resulting prototype look noticeably more impressive and polished during a stakeholder demo
Loop count, as a consideration, should genuinely never factor at all into how a team chooses its fidelity level
items.explanation: The trade-off is real, but sometimes unavoidable: if a question can only be answered at a certain fidelity (like interaction feel), running many cheap loops that can't test the real risk isn't actually faster — it just delays finding out.
items.reference:
A fixed timeline holds more short loops than long ones — loop length trades directly against how many chances you get to catch a mistake.

Why: a shorter loop isn't just cheaper per round — it buys more rounds inside the same deadline.

items.prompt: Which of these can a low-fidelity click-through prototype NOT honestly test?
choices: Whether the overall order of steps in the flow makes basic logical sense to a first-time user trying it out
Whether the actual wording and copy used on a given screen reads clearly and makes sense to a first-time user
Whether an animation's timing feels smooth on a slow device
Whether a given screen in the flow is obviously missing a step that a first-time user would clearly expect to see
items.explanation: Structural and wording questions are exactly what low fidelity is good at. Real animation timing under real device conditions is a behavior question that a static or click-through prototype simply has no way to reproduce.
items.reference:
🎬 Real motion / animation timing
📶 Real network latency
🗄️ Real data volume and edge cases

Why: these three specifically require something running under real or near-real conditions — no lower-fidelity substitute reproduces them.

items.prompt: A team wants to know if a search feature stays fast with a real, messy production dataset. Why can't a low-fidelity prototype with 10 clean sample rows answer this?
choices: It genuinely can — the overall size of the sample dataset used never actually matters for this kind of question
Because performance and messy real-world edge cases only show up under real or near-real data and conditions, which a small clean sample doesn't reproduce
Because low-fidelity prototypes are, by some unwritten rule, never actually allowed to be built using sample data
Because this specific question is, on closer inspection, actually a structural question rather than a performance one
items.explanation: Performance and data-messiness questions depend on conditions a tiny clean sample can't recreate. Only testing against something closer to real data and real scale will surface the slowdowns and edge cases that matter.
items.reference:
🎬 Real motion / animation timing
📶 Real network latency
🗄️ Real data volume and edge cases

Why: these three specifically require something running under real or near-real conditions — no lower-fidelity substitute reproduces them.

items.prompt: Going from a wireframe to a clickable prototype costs roughly 2-3x more. Going from clickable to coded costs roughly 3x more again. What does this tell you about where the best cost-to-confidence trade tends to sit?
choices: At the very top of the spectrum — a fully coded prototype is always the best possible trade since it's the most trustworthy
Usually somewhere in the middle of the spectrum, since the steepest cost jump (clickable to coded) buys a comparatively small increase in signal quality
At the very bottom of the spectrum — plain paper sketches always give the best possible trade regardless of the question
Cost and signal quality rise at precisely the same steady rate throughout, so there's no meaningful trade-off to speak of
items.explanation: Cost and signal quality don't rise together at the same rate — cost accelerates faster than trustworthiness does, especially near the top of the spectrum. That's why the best value is usually found before the most expensive step, not at it.
items.reference:
Cost rises much faster than signal quality as fidelity climbs — the biggest cost jump (clickable → coded) buys the smallest gain in trustworthiness.

Why: most of the achievable confidence is available several rungs below the most expensive option.

items.prompt: A teammate argues 'we should always build the coded version, since it always gives the most trustworthy answer.' What's the flaw in using that as a blanket rule?
choices: There's genuinely no flaw in that reasoning at all — a more trustworthy result is always worth it regardless of its cost
It ignores that the extra trustworthiness a coded build buys over a clickable one is often small relative to its much larger cost, and that many questions don't need that extra trustworthiness at all
Coded prototypes are, in actual practice, typically considered noticeably less trustworthy overall than clickable ones
This particular flaw genuinely only ever applies in situations where the team happens to have an unlimited timeline
items.explanation: Trustworthiness and cost don't move in lockstep — the last, most expensive step often buys the smallest marginal gain. And plenty of questions (purely structural ones) don't need that gain in the first place.
items.reference:
Cost rises much faster than signal quality as fidelity climbs — the biggest cost jump (clickable → coded) buys the smallest gain in trustworthiness.

Why: most of the achievable confidence is available several rungs below the most expensive option.

items.prompt: What is 'signal quality' referring to, in the trade-off between fidelity and cost?
choices: How visually attractive, polished, and professional-looking the resulting prototype ends up appearing once it's finished
How much you can trust that the test's result predicts what will actually happen with the real, finished product
How quickly the team was actually able to construct and finish putting together the prototype in the first place
The total number of people on the team who reviewed and signed off on the prototype internally before it was ever tested
items.explanation: Signal quality is about trustworthiness of the result — how confidently a test's outcome predicts real-world behavior once the feature is actually built and shipped, not how the prototype looks or how quickly it was made.
items.reference:
Cost rises much faster than signal quality as fidelity climbs — the biggest cost jump (clickable → coded) buys the smallest gain in trustworthiness.

Why: most of the achievable confidence is available several rungs below the most expensive option.

items.prompt: What was the actual mistake the checkout team made — was it building a bad flow, or something else?
choices: Building a genuinely bad flow — the reordered checkout idea itself turned out to simply be the wrong design choice
Picking a fidelity level (coded, live-wired) that made being wrong maximally expensive, for a question that a cheap prototype could have answered just as well
Testing the redesigned flow with far too many real users at once, which ended up muddying the resulting feedback
Failing to document the redesigned checkout flow clearly enough for the rest of the engineering team to follow along
items.explanation: The redesigned flow later worked once fixed — the flaw wasn't the idea, it was the cost of finding out it needed fixing. A structural question ('does this order make sense') never needed a coded, live-wired build to answer.
items.reference:
💻 Built coded version first — 3 weeks
❌ Users got lost — flow order confusing
💸 All 3 weeks discarded

Why: the question was purely structural — a 2-day clickable prototype could have caught the same problem for a fraction of the cost.

items.prompt: The checkout team reasoned that 'a sketch or click-through wouldn't tell us anything real.' What was wrong with that reasoning?
choices: Nothing was actually wrong with that reasoning — they were entirely right, and building the coded test was genuinely necessary
The question they needed answered (does the new order make sense to a first-time user) was structural, and a click-through answers structural questions just as validly as coded code does
Click-through prototypes like the one in question can, as a strict rule, never be shown to any real users at all
The reasoning was actually correct, but only for interaction-feel questions specifically — not for this one here, which is exactly the point the team missed
items.explanation: Their reasoning conflated 'realistic-looking' with 'able to answer the question.' For a structural question, a click-through's fidelity is entirely sufficient — the flow's order doesn't depend on real code running underneath it.
items.reference:
💻 Built coded version first — 3 weeks
❌ Users got lost — flow order confusing
💸 All 3 weeks discarded

Why: the question was purely structural — a 2-day clickable prototype could have caught the same problem for a fraction of the cost.

items.prompt: If the checkout team had run a 2-day clickable prototype first and gotten the same 'confusing' result, what would have been different about the outcome?
choices: Nothing at all would have been different here — the flow would still have needed redesigning either way regardless
The same information would have arrived on day 3 instead of week 4, at a fraction of the cost, leaving time to redesign and retest inside the original schedule
A clickable prototype simply cannot reveal the exact same kind of user confusion that a fully coded version is able to
The team would still have needed to go ahead and build the full coded version anyway, just to confirm the finding
items.explanation: The result — 'the flow is confusing' — was identical either way. What changed is when it arrived and what it cost: days and near-zero cost instead of weeks and three weeks of discarded engineering, with enough schedule left to fix and retest.
items.reference:
💻 Built coded version first — 3 weeks
❌ Users got lost — flow order confusing
💸 All 3 weeks discarded

Why: the question was purely structural — a 2-day clickable prototype could have caught the same problem for a fraction of the cost.

items.prompt: The drag-reorder team got 8 positive reactions from their click-through test. Why were those reactions 'real and meaningless at the same time'?
choices: Because the eight users tested were, in this specific case, simply lying outright in order to be polite to the team
Because the feedback was honest, but about a version of the feature that couldn't fail the way the real, coded version later did — the actual risk was never present in the test
Because a sample size of only eight total users is, on its own, generally considered far too small to trust here
Because click-through prototypes like this one should, as a rule, never actually be tested with any real users at all
items.explanation: The users genuinely liked what they saw — that part was real. But what they saw had no real drag motion in it, so their approval said nothing about the lag and overshoot that only existed in the coded version, which is what actually caused the failure.
items.reference:
🖱️ Tested with instant-jump click-through
👍 8 users said it 'worked great'
🐌 Real version had lag + overshoot
📉 Users abandoned mid-gesture after shipping

Why: a click-through can't reproduce real motion, so it couldn't have caught a problem that lives entirely in real motion.

items.prompt: What type of question was 'will this drag interaction feel good,' and why did that make the low-fidelity test the wrong tool?
choices: A structural question — in this case, the team had simply gone ahead and tested the entirely wrong flow by mistake
An interaction-feel question — it required real, running motion to test at all, which a click-through by definition doesn't have
A performance question — in this case, the team genuinely needed to go ahead and test it using more realistic data
There's genuinely no meaningful category that applies here at all; in truth any fidelity level should have worked fine
items.explanation: Interaction-feel questions depend on real motion and timing existing in the test itself. A click-through fakes only destinations, not the movement in between — so it structurally cannot answer a question about how motion feels.
items.reference:
🖱️ Tested with instant-jump click-through
👍 8 users said it 'worked great'
🐌 Real version had lag + overshoot
📉 Users abandoned mid-gesture after shipping

Why: a click-through can't reproduce real motion, so it couldn't have caught a problem that lives entirely in real motion.

items.prompt: Compared to the checkout team's mistake, what makes the drag team's mistake the 'quieter' failure mode?
choices: It genuinely isn't quieter at all in this case — both of these two failures actually looked completely identical at the time
Because it produced confident, positive-looking results at test time, so nothing appeared wrong until real users hit the gap after shipping
Because the overall number of users involved in running this particular drag-reorder test happened to be noticeably smaller
Because the drag-reorder team, in this particular case, actually never ran any kind of usability test at all beforehand
items.explanation: The checkout team's mistake was visible immediately — the test came back negative. The drag team's mistake looked like success right up until shipping, because the test genuinely couldn't have surfaced the real problem — false confidence is harder to catch than an obvious bad result.
items.reference:
🖱️ Tested with instant-jump click-through
👍 8 users said it 'worked great'
🐌 Real version had lag + overshoot
📉 Users abandoned mid-gesture after shipping

Why: a click-through can't reproduce real motion, so it couldn't have caught a problem that lives entirely in real motion.

items.prompt: A team wants to know whether a new dashboard's chart labels are understandable at a glance. What's the appropriate minimum fidelity, and why?
choices: Coded, fully real-time production data — this particular question is fundamentally about raw system performance
A static wireframe or paper sketch — this is a structural/wording question, not one about motion or real data
A prototype built with real, functioning drag interaction — chart labels, in this framing, always require motion to properly test
No prototype of any fidelity whatsoever is actually capable of testing basic chart label clarity in this situation
items.explanation: Reading and understanding labels doesn't depend on real motion, real data volume, or real latency — it's a wording/structural question, which a static wireframe answers just as validly as a coded build would.

Ask firstThen pick
What type of question is this?The minimum fidelity that type requires

items.prompt: A team wants to know if a pull-to-refresh gesture on a list feels natural, including the timing of when it triggers. What's the appropriate minimum fidelity, and why?

items.prompt: The checkout team had roughly 4 weeks before their launch decision and used a loop that took all 4 weeks to produce a first answer. What did that cost them, beyond the 3 weeks of code?
choices: Nothing at all beyond the underlying code itself — in this case the code was genuinely the only real cost incurred
Any chance to run a second loop and fix the problem inside the original schedule — the slow loop consumed the entire available time in a single, failed attempt
It permanently cost them the underlying ability to ever meaningfully redesign the checkout flow again at any later point
It ultimately cost them nothing at all in the end, since the redesigned flow did end up working fine later anyway
items.explanation: Beyond the wasted engineering hours, the real cost was schedule: a loop that consumes the entire available window in one attempt leaves zero room to act on what's learned, forcing either a blown deadline or shipping something known to be broken.

6-week timeline ÷ 3-week loop = 1 chance. Same timeline ÷ 2-day loop = several chances.

Why: loop length directly sets how many times a team can afford to be wrong and still recover.

Short feedback loops, as a rule, only really matter when a project's deadline happens to be loose rather than tight
items.explanation: The tighter the deadline, the fewer loops fit inside it regardless of length — which makes each loop's length matter more, since a single slow loop can consume the entire remaining runway with no time left to act on the result.
